activities.anchor: the stain's colour predicts which drugs
activities.caption: file each fact with its pathogen family
activities.name: iaFamiliesBuckets

config.prompt: The family name decides the weapon — file each fact:

items.label: own machinery — wall, ribosomes, DNA — every part a potential drug target
sorted by the Gram stain: thick peptidoglycan holds the purple dye
genetic payloads in protein coats, with no metabolism of their own
antivirals target viral enzymes with minimal human counterparts — acyclovir, oseltamivir
drugs must aim at cell walls and ergosterol membranes (amphotericin, azoles)
the hardest to treat selectively, because the exploitable differences are few

config.why: Which is why the clinician's first question is "which family" and the second is "which machinery does it depend on" — the first treatment is usually empiric, narrowed once cultures return.

activities.anchor: the treatment always has two targets
activities.caption: fill the host-response picture
activities.name: iaHostCloze

config.text: Much of "feeling ill" is the host's own response: fever is a regulated %%0%% set-point shift that many pathogens replicate poorly above, and inflammation is %%1%% plumbing that delivers phagocytes to the site. The catastrophic failure mode is %%2%% — the response becoming dysregulated and systemic — which is why antibiotics and fluids within the first %%3%% measurably change survival.
config.hint: Two body words, one syndrome, one unit of time.

activities.caption: pair each antibiotic class with its target
activities.name: iaTargetsMatch

config.prompt: Selective toxicity, class by class — pair each drug family with what it attacks:

pairs.right: block peptidoglycan cross-links — the cell-wall target, the oldest and safest
bind the 30S or 50S ribosomal subunits and freeze translation
block folate synthesis — a pathway humans lack, since we eat folate

config.why: Every target is a piece of bacterial machinery human cells either lack or carry in a different form — and bactericidal drugs kill while bacteriostatic ones halt growth and let immunity finish.

activities.caption: one line of the resistance briefing misreads the projection
activities.name: iaProjectionSpot

config.prompt: A resistance briefing — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: Beta-lactamase enzymes cleave penicillins — hence clavulanic acid added as a decoy inhibitor.
Efflux pumps eject the drug faster than it enters.
MRSA carries PBP2a, an altered enzyme beta-lactams can no longer bind — target modification.
Reduced porin channels and biofilm matrices shield whole communities — impermeability.
The O'Neill review projected drug-resistant infections would kill about one million people a year by 2050 — below today's road-injury toll.
config.correction: The O'Neill review (2016) projected 10 million deaths a year by 2050 — more than cancer — at a cumulative cost near 100 trillion dollars.
config.why: The four mechanisms are concrete; the projection is why stewardship is policy rather than etiquette.

activities.anchor: a drug that once worked for you can fail you later
activities.caption: bet the early-stopping question before the reveal
activities.name: iaStopPredict

config.q: A patient completes half the course, feels better, and saves the rest "for next time". What does early stopping actually do?
choices: It protects the body from becoming resistant.
It leaves the partially-resistant survivors standing in the bacterial population.
It has no effect on resistance either way.
It makes the person allergic to the drug.
config.why: Bodies do not become resistant — bacteria do. Stopping early kills the most susceptible organisms and trains the rest: the same error, run in reverse from the prescription pad.

config.root: The prescriber's pen is itself an ecological force.

start.text: Cultures are pending, the patient is stable, the likely organism is uncertain. What does stewardship prescribe?

choices.label: The narrowest-spectrum agent that covers the likely organisms
choices.feedback: Empiric-but-narrow: cover the probable pathogens, spare the commensal reservoirs.

choices.label: The broadest agent available, to be safe
choices.feedback: Broad coverage treats this patient — and selects every other bacterium on the ward.

narrow.text: Narrow-spectrum coverage plus de-escalation when cultures return is the stewardship pattern: treat the likely organism now, narrow the moment the laboratory answers.

choices.label: Now: the dose and the finish

broad.text: Over-broad dosing and under-dosing both select hardest — the first by exposing everything, the second by leaving partially-resistant survivors. Correct dosing kills the population before it can multiply.

choices.label: Now: the dose and the finish

dose.text: Dose correctly and stop when the course is done — no survivors left to train. And the discipline extends past the prescription: by weight, most of the world's antibiotic tonnage is used in livestock, so resistance genes travel in food, water and people.

config.why: Treat only bacterial infections, narrow the spectrum, dose correctly, de-escalate, stop when done — stewardship is genuinely a one-world problem.

activities.anchor: the only human disease ever eradicated
activities.caption: drag between the two platform families
activities.name: iaVaccineCompare

config.prompt: Vaccine platforms trade memory against safety — drag between them:

before.label: live attenuated (measles, oral polio, BCG)
before.text: Replicates mildly: the strongest, longest memory — at the price of caution in immunocompromised patients.

after.label: inactivated / subunit (flu, hepatitis B, acellular pertussis)
after.text: Safer but weaker — needs adjuvants and boosters to finish the immune education.

config.why: Toxoids train antibodies against the toxin rather than the bug; mRNA and viral-vector platforms deliver just the antigen's blueprint — change the sequence, change the target, and development collapses from years to months.

activities.anchor: waits for its competitors to be cleared
activities.caption: call the FMT cure rate
activities.name: iaFmtEstimate

config.prompt: Broad-spectrum antibiotics dynamite the resident flora, and C. difficile blooms in the vacancy. Faecal microbiota transplantation cures recurrent C. difficile at rates above roughly what?
config.why: Above 80% — one of modern medicine's strangest and most effective therapies: restoring the flora wholesale instead of fighting the spore-former with yet another drug.
config.context: The microbiome is not scenery: it colonises surfaces pathogens would love, trains the immune system and synthesises vitamins.
